title: Can New Technologies Finally Replace Animal Testing?
gist: Regulators (FDA Modernization Act 2.0, FDA's 2025 pledge and September 2026 'nonclinical tests' rule, NIH, EU, UK, OECD) are opening the door to nonanimal methods such as organs-on-chips and in silico models, and early validation data (Emulate liver chip ~7/8 hits; heart simulations 89% vs 75% for animals) are promising. But costly context-specific validation, lack of standardization and deep cultural inertia mean adoption is more a change-management problem than a technology one.

themes.theme: Regulatory pivot away from animal testing

insights.claim: The FDA recently denied a pharmaceutical company permission to run a clinical trial because it presented animal data while the agency wanted data from organs-on-a-chip or a comparable alternative, according to TissUse executive Ilka Maschmeyer.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Signals regulators may now actively demand NAM data, creating pull demand for organ-chip vendors.
insights.quote: The problem: It had presented animal data, but the FDA wanted data from organs-on-a-chip or some comparable alternative.
insights.locator: A recent story told by Ilka

insights.claim: The FDA Modernization Act 2.0, passed in late 2022, explicitly authorized new approach methodologies (NAMs) in preclinical studies required before human trials, ending the prior mandate for animal testing.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Removed the legal barrier to NAM-based IND packages, opening a regulated market for alternatives.
insights.quote: It explicitly authorized the use of NAMs in the preclinical studies required of new drugs before they could enter human trials.
insights.locator: Yet even as studies piled up

insights.claim: In 2025 the FDA pledged to make animal studies the exception rather than the norm for drug safety testing.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Policy direction implies structural shrinkage of animal-testing demand in drug safety work.
insights.quote: In 2025, the FDA pledged “to make animal studies the exception rather than the norm” for drug safety testing.

insights.claim: In September 2026 the FDA issued a rule that, if it takes effect, will replace references to 'animal tests' in drug-development regulations with 'nonclinical tests', explicitly allowing validated human-cell systems, organs-on-chips and computer models.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Codifies NAM acceptance in regulation text; a near-term catalyst for organ-chip and in silico modeling providers.

insights.claim: In 2025 the U.S. National Institutes of Health, the world's largest public biomedical research funder, began requiring grant applicants studying animal models to also incorporate nonanimal research such as real-world data or NAM studies.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Grant-driven mandate expands the academic customer base for NAM tools and services.

insights.claim: The European Commission and the United Kingdom have announced plans to phase out animal testing, and the OECD updated its guidelines to allow expanded use of NAMs.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
entities: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
insights.so_what: Multi-jurisdiction alignment reduces regulatory fragmentation risk for NAM vendors selling globally.

insights.claim: Regulatory acceptance is the main driver of NAM adoption: TissUse sees clients increasingly coming from animal-model researchers who now must add in vitro models, a shift Maschmeyer traces mainly to regulatory change.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Demand for organ-chip platforms is regulation-led, making policy milestones the key leading indicator.
insights.quote: “It’s more people who are working with animal models who now have to also add in vitro models.”

insights.claim: Maschmeyer predicts that regulators requesting NAM data instead of animal data, still rare today, will become more and more frequent.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Points to accelerating demand for NAM-generated regulatory data packages.
insights.quote: “It’s rare still,” says Maschmeyer, “but I think it’s going to be more and more frequent.”
insights.locator: The moment spoke to a trend

insights.claim: An estimated 92 percent of drugs entering U.S. clinical trials fail to reach the market, often because they prove ineffective or unsafe in ways animal experiments did not predict, with even higher failure rates in heart disease, cancer and brain disease.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Better-predictive preclinical tools could materially cut R&D attrition, the biggest cost driver in pharma.
insights.quote: An estimated 92 percent of all drugs that enter U.S. clinical trials fail to reach the market

insights.claim: Animal experiments can produce false negatives as well as false positives, and some researchers argue aspirin or acetaminophen might have been abandoned under modern testing requirements.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Implies animal-based screening may be discarding viable drug candidates, a hidden value leak in pipelines.

insights.claim: The author cautions that high clinical failure rates are not automatically due to reliance on animals, since flawed study designs and disease complexity also contribute.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations that NAMs alone will fix drug attrition.
insights.quote: These statistics don’t automatically mean that a reliance on animals is to blame.

insights.claim: Harvard Wyss Institute's lung-on-a-chip, led by Donald Ingber, mechanically 'breathed' and reacted to inflammatory proteins and bacteria much as living lungs do; Science initially rejected the paper and required mouse experiments before publishing it in 2010.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Illustrates how entrenched the animal-data default was and how far acceptance has shifted.

insights.claim: The 2010 lung-on-a-chip paper has been cited by nearly 5,400 other papers.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Indicates the scale of the academic field built on organ-chip technology.
insights.quote: (It has since been cited by nearly 5,400 other papers.)

insights.claim: NAMs now include organoids, organ-on-a-chip systems for brains, hearts, kidneys and placentas, and multi-organ systems linking as many as 10 organs that recapitulate human physiology better than a mouse or monkey, though not perfectly.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Defines the product categories in a growing NAM market.
insights.quote: As many as 10 such organs have been linked together

insights.claim: Computational simulations and AI tools that analyze data from other NAM systems and inform future experiments form an iterative loop supporting the wet-lab platforms.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: AI/in silico layers are a software-margin opportunity atop hardware organ-chip platforms.
insights.quote: a high-powered iterative loop

insights.claim: ESQlabs builds digital-twin systems in which organ-chip data inform whole-human simulations of drug outcomes and disease progression.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Example of chip-plus-simulation integration as a business model.

insights.claim: Greenstone Biosciences, cofounded by Stanford's Joseph Wu, uses stem-cell-derived human tissues and AI to model disease and predict drug responses, and freely shares its stem-cell line library with academic researchers.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Open-sharing strategies may be used to seed ecosystems and future commercial demand.

insights.claim: An Emulate liver-on-a-chip correctly flagged about seven of every eight drugs that had safely passed animal trials but proved toxic to human livers.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that organ chips can catch toxicity animals miss, supporting commercial value claims.
insights.quote: a liver-on-a-chip system from Emulate correctly flagged about seven out of every eight drugs

insights.claim: Oxford University and Janssen Pharmaceutica researchers showed computational simulations of human heart cells flagged arrhythmia-causing compounds with 89 percent accuracy versus 75 percent for animal studies.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: In silico cardiotoxicity models outperforming animals strengthens the case for software-based safety testing.
insights.quote: flagged compounds that caused a type of dangerous heart arrhythmia with 89 percent accuracy, compared to animal studies that were 75 percent accurate

insights.claim: Emulate's liver-chip validation study required 870 chips and the labor of 16 full-time employees for 16 weeks, and each new context of use, such as large-molecule rather than small-molecule drugs, would need another such study.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Context-specific validation costs are a barrier to entry that favors well-capitalized vendors.
insights.quote: Emulate’s study required 870 chips and the labor equivalent of 16 full-time employees working for 16 weeks

insights.claim: Because comparable validation studies would be needed for every commercial NAM and every context of use, small companies cannot afford validation, according to Safer Medicines Trust founder Kathy Archibald.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Implies consolidation pressure and a moat for incumbents with validated platforms.
insights.quote: “It takes too long and costs too much, and small companies can’t afford to do it.”

insights.claim: Ingber argues that academic organ chips will not change FDA uptake unless they become mass-produced commercial products meeting fine performance criteria and giving the same results anywhere in the world.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Value accrues to companies that can industrialize and standardize chips, not to academic prototypes.
insights.quote: It has to be a commercial product. It has to be mass-produced and meet very fine performance criteria
insights.locator: You read about all the organ

insights.claim: Even minute variations in hydrogel scaffolds can produce very different tissue growth in organ chips, and differing metrics across groups hamper adoption of vascularized tumor-on-a-chip platforms, making standardization of workflows and reporting essential.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Standardization and automated culture systems are key differentiators and potential bottlenecks.
insights.locator: You read about all the organ

insights.claim: Even with instructions, industry users of Emulate chips still need coaching from Ingber's lab on the finer points of tending stem-cell cultures.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Usability and training burdens slow scaling and create services revenue opportunities.
insights.locator: Workflows and procedures need to be

insights.claim: NAM proponents say much of the preclinical and clinical data needed for comparisons is proprietary, and the FDA has called for an open-access repository of drug toxicity data.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Data access is a gating factor; a public toxicity repository could accelerate AI/in silico NAMs.

insights.claim: Ingber says academic scientists should collaborate more with industry on NAMs with government funding, and Hartung suggests running new animal experiments in parallel with NAMs for side-by-side comparisons.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Points to potential public funding flows into NAM validation.

insights.claim: ESQlabs' Christian Maass says the field has not yet proven NAMs perform better than or as well as animal models, and that an iPhone-like 'aha' moment from head-to-head comparisons is still lacking.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: An insider admits the evidence gap; adoption risk remains until decisive comparative data emerge.
insights.quote: researchers have not yet provided “the evidence and the proof that we are doing better or as good as the animal models.”

insights.claim: Most NAMs have yet to be rigorously tested, though early studies suggest their potential.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Investors should discount NAM performance claims pending validation.
insights.quote: Most NAMs have yet to be rigorously tested, but early studies suggest their potential.

insights.claim: Johns Hopkins toxicologist Thomas Hartung argues the shift to NAMs is more about change management than technology.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Adoption timelines are governed by institutional behavior, not technical readiness, so expect slower uptake than tech progress suggests.
insights.quote: “It is more about change management than it is about the technology.”

insights.claim: The monocyte activation test, validated in the mid-1990s to replace the rabbit pyrogen test, was not accepted by the European Pharmacopeia until 2010, and rabbits are still widely used for the test worldwide.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Historical precedent: validated replacements can take 15+ years to be accepted and still not fully displace animals.
insights.quote: And rabbits are still widely used for this test worldwide.

insights.claim: Even after formal animal-testing requirements disappear, regulators, grant reviewers, peer reviewers and journal editors often still informally expect animal data, according to Kathrin Herrmann.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
entities: Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing
insights.so_what: Residual demand for animal studies may persist despite regulatory change, slowing displacement of incumbent CRO animal work.
insights.quote: “The formal requirement may disappear, but the informal expectation persists,”

insights.claim: Early-career researchers report NAM-only proposals are seen as risky by funders, face pressure to add animal experiments for credibility, have limited access to NAM infrastructure, and face uncertain careers.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Infrastructure access and funding norms are bottlenecks that could be addressed by shared-facility or service models.
insights.locator: Herrmann is now overseeing a survey

insights.claim: Scientists whose identities, skills and lab jobs are built on animal models may resist NAMs, especially when human well-being or millions of dollars ride on the choice.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Incumbent workforce resistance is a structural drag on NAM adoption.
insights.quote: “I could see why it’s a hard thing for people to take it up,”

insights.claim: Generational turnover via training is expected to drive adoption: Hartung's Coursera modules have reached about 12,000 students, and Stanford's Joseph Wu predicts trainees will replace the old guard.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Suggests a multi-year, generational adoption curve rather than a sudden switch.
insights.quote: “These trainees will set up their own labs. They will go to industry. They will replace the old guard,”

insights.claim: Early-stage drug development and regulatory testing account for roughly 30 percent of animals used in experiments, with the rest used in basic biological research where replacement is less straightforward.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: The near-term addressable displacement is a minority of animal use; basic research is a larger, harder market.
insights.quote: Early-stage drug development and regulatory testing account for roughly 30 percent of animals used in experiments

insights.claim: Hartung sees NAM adoption in toxicology as a 'lighthouse function' guiding other research areas, and says 'suddenly, all the dams have opened'.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Toxicology success could expand NAM use into basic research, enlarging the long-term market.
insights.quote: “Suddenly, all the dams have opened,” he says.

insights.claim: Ingber cites organ-on-a-chip insights into inflammatory bowel disease, preterm birth and viral infection treatment that could not have been made in animals.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/48576411181
insights.so_what: Shows NAMs can generate novel biology, not just replace tests, supporting discovery-stage use cases.
